_about: App Rescue topic bank. One entry per episode; an entry is burned once published. Every field is the ONLY set of facts the writer may state about the problem. Keep entries to failure modes that are well documented and true of AI-built apps in general -- never a client story, never a statistic. Add entries freely; ids must stay unique and stable. Optional per-format fields: `check` (2-3 steps a founder runs on THEIR OWN app, dashboard or own test accounts only), `prompts` + `prompt_fails` (what founders typically ask the AI and why that cannot fix it), `checklist` (one launch-checklist line). `checklist_order` sets the launch checklist's numbering.

topics.topic: Your Supabase tables are readable by anyone because Row Level Security is off
symptoms: Anyone can read every user's rows
topics.cause: The Supabase anon key ships inside every browser by design. Row Level Security is what stops it reading every row. With RLS off on a table, any visitor can query that whole table straight from the browser console.
fixes: Turn RLS on for every table
Write a policy per table: users only see their own rows
Test it logged out and as a second user
check: Open Supabase, go to Table Editor
Look for tables marked 'RLS disabled'
Any table holding user data must say enabled
prompts: Only show users their own data
topics.prompt_fails: The AI can filter what each screen displays, but the database still hands every row to anyone who asks. The rule has to live in the database.
topics.checklist: Row Level Security is on for every table

topics.topic: You turned on Row Level Security and now your app shows no data at all
symptoms: The AI keeps rewriting the frontend
topics.cause: With RLS enabled and no policy, Postgres denies every read and returns an empty result, not an error. The bug is in the database rules, so editing the screens never fixes it.
fixes: Add a select policy that matches who should see the row
Add separate insert and update policies
Check the user id column the policy compares against
check: Open Supabase, go to Authentication, then Policies
Find tables with RLS on and no policies
Those tables return nothing to anyone
prompts: The list is empty, fix it
topics.prompt_fails: The AI looks at the screen that shows the empty list and rewrites it. The screen is fine; the database is refusing to answer.

topics.topic: The Supabase service role key is in your frontend code
symptoms: The key is visible in the browser
topics.cause: The service role key bypasses Row Level Security completely. It is meant for servers only. If it is in frontend code, anyone who opens dev tools has full read and write access to your database.
fixes: Rotate the key in the Supabase dashboard today
Move privileged work into an Edge Function or server
Use only the anon key in the browser
check: Search your code for 'service_role'
Open your live site, then dev tools, then Sources
If that key appears in the browser, rotate it now
topics.prompt_fails: Using the all-powerful key makes the error disappear, so the AI reaches for it. The error was the security working.
topics.checklist: No service role key anywhere in the browser

topics.topic: Your API keys are public because of how frontend environment variables work
symptoms: Strange charges on your OpenAI or Stripe account
topics.cause: In Vite apps, any variable starting with VITE_ is compiled into the JavaScript the browser downloads. Next.js does the same for NEXT_PUBLIC_. A secret key with that prefix is published to every visitor.
fixes: Rotate every exposed key
Call paid APIs from a server or Edge Function
Keep only publishable keys in the browser
check: List your environment variables
Any secret with VITE_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_ in front is public
Search your live site's JavaScript for the key
prompts: Put the key in the .env file
topics.prompt_fails: Moving a key into .env feels like hiding it, but with that prefix the build tool copies it straight back into the browser.
topics.checklist: No secret keys in public environment variables

topics.topic: Your app calls the OpenAI API straight from the browser
symptoms: Usage bill climbing with no new users
topics.cause: If the browser calls the AI API directly, the API key travels with every request, and anyone can copy it from the network tab and run up your bill.
fixes: Move the call behind your own server endpoint
Rotate the key
Add per-user rate limits
check: Open your live app with dev tools, Network tab
Use your AI feature once
Your key in a request to the AI provider means it's public
topics.prompt_fails: The quickest way to make the feature work is to call the AI from the browser, so that is what gets built. It works, and it hands out your key.
topics.checklist: Paid APIs are only called from your server

topics.topic: Your app unlocks paid features when someone visits the Stripe success page
symptoms: Some users have Pro without paying
topics.cause: A success page URL can be opened by anyone, paid or not. The trustworthy signal is Stripe's webhook, sent server to server and checked with a signing secret.
fixes: Grant access only from a verified Stripe webhook
Verify the webhook signature
Handle refunds and failed renewals too
check: Log in with a test account that never paid
Visit your payment success URL directly
If that unlocks paid features, anyone can do it
prompts: Give users Pro after they pay
Unlock features on the success page
topics.prompt_fails: Unlocking on the success page is the simplest thing that passes a quick test. It is also something anyone can visit without paying.
topics.checklist: Paid access is granted only by a verified Stripe webhook

topics.topic: Your Stripe webhook accepts any request without checking the signature
symptoms: No signature check in the code
topics.cause: Stripe signs every webhook with a secret. If your endpoint does not verify that signature, anyone who finds the URL can send a fake payment event and get access for free.
fixes: Verify the Stripe-Signature header with your webhook secret
Reject anything that fails
Log every event you process
check: Find your Stripe webhook handler
Look for a signature check using your webhook secret
No check means the endpoint trusts anyone
topics.prompt_fails: A webhook that skips the signature check works in every test, so nothing tells the AI it is missing.
topics.checklist: Every webhook checks its signature

topics.topic: Your checkout trusts the price the browser sends
symptoms: A user could change it to one cent
topics.cause: Anything the browser sends can be edited. If the server creates the checkout with an amount supplied by the page, a user can change it before paying.
fixes: Look up the price on the server from a product or price id
Use Stripe Price objects
Never accept amounts from the client
check: Find where checkout is created
See where the amount comes from
If it comes from the page, the user controls the price
prompts: Pass the cart total to Stripe
topics.prompt_fails: Sending the total from the page is the shortest path to a working checkout. The AI is solving 'make it work', not 'make it safe'.
topics.checklist: Prices are looked up on the server, never sent by the page

topics.topic: Your admin page is only hidden, not protected
symptoms: Admin link hidden for normal users
isAdmin flag checked in the browser
Admin actions still work if called directly
topics.cause: Hiding a button is not security. If the database and API do not check the user's role, anyone can call the admin actions directly or flip the flag in the browser.
fixes: Check roles in the database or server, not the UI
Store roles where users cannot edit them
Test admin endpoints as a normal user
check: Log in as a normal test user
Try opening your admin page's address directly
Check whether admin actions still succeed
prompts: Only show the admin page to admins
topics.prompt_fails: 'Only show it to admins' gets you a hidden button. Protection is a separate rule on the server, and nobody asked for it.
topics.checklist: Admin actions are checked on the server, not just hidden

topics.topic: Your password reset and signup emails send people to localhost
symptoms: Users click the email link and get an error page
topics.cause: Supabase Auth builds email links from its Site URL and allowed redirect URLs. If those still point at your development address, real users land on a page that does not exist.
fixes: Set the Site URL to your real domain
Add every production and preview URL to the redirect list
Send yourself a reset email on the live site
check: Open Supabase, Authentication, URL Configuration
Check the Site URL is your real domain
Send yourself a password reset on the live site
topics.prompt_fails: The links are built from a setting in your auth dashboard, not from your code, so code changes cannot fix them.
topics.checklist: Auth emails link to your real domain

topics.topic: Google login works in the preview and breaks on your real domain
symptoms: Login with Google fails on the live site
topics.cause: Google only sends users back to redirect URLs you registered. A new domain that is not on the list is rejected, and the builder's preview URL is usually the only one registered.
fixes: Add the production callback URL in Google Cloud
Add it in Supabase Auth too
Test login on the real domain before launch
check: Try Google login on your real domain
Open Google Cloud, Credentials, your OAuth client
Confirm your production callback URL is listed
topics.prompt_fails: The allowed addresses live in Google's console, outside your code. The AI can only change the code.
topics.checklist: Login works on your real domain, not just the preview

topics.topic: Every fix the AI makes breaks something else
topics.cause: The AI edits the files it is shown, not the whole system. When one root cause shows up in several places, patching each symptom creates new conflicts instead of removing the cause.
fixes: Stop prompting and get the code into GitHub
Find the one root cause
Fix it once, then add a test so it stays fixed
check: Count how many prompts the last bug took
Note whether each fix broke something new
Three or more in a row means a root cause, not bad luck
prompts: That broke something else, fix it again
topics.prompt_fails: Each prompt shows the AI a few files and one symptom. When the cause is shared across the app, every local fix moves the problem instead of removing it.

topics.topic: You have no way to undo the change that broke your app
topics.cause: Without version control there is no record of what changed or a clean way back. Connecting the project to GitHub keeps every change and lets you roll back to the last working state.
fixes: Connect the project to GitHub
Commit before every big prompt
Roll back instead of re-prompting
check: Check whether your project is connected to GitHub
Look for a history of changes you can restore
No history means no clean way back
prompts: Go back to how it was yesterday
topics.prompt_fails: Asking the AI to undo means asking it to rewrite from memory. A real rollback restores the exact files that worked.
topics.checklist: The project is in GitHub with a working history

topics.topic: Your app works in the builder and shows a blank page once deployed
symptoms: Console says a variable is undefined
topics.cause: Environment variables set in the builder are not automatically copied to your host. Without them the app cannot reach its database or APIs, and often renders nothing at all.
fixes: Add every environment variable in your host's settings
Redeploy after adding them
Check the browser console on the live site
check: Open your live site's browser console
Look for 'undefined' or missing key errors
Compare your host's environment variables with the builder's
topics.prompt_fails: The code is fine; the settings never reached your host. The AI cannot see your host's settings page.
topics.checklist: Every environment variable is set on your host

topics.topic: Your users' uploaded files are public to anyone with the link
symptoms: Private documents openable without logging in
topics.cause: A public storage bucket serves every file to anyone who has or guesses the URL. Private files need a private bucket and short-lived signed URLs.
fixes: Make the bucket private
Serve files with signed URLs that expire
Add storage policies per user
check: Open Supabase, then Storage
See which buckets are marked public
Private documents should never be in a public bucket
topics.prompt_fails: A public bucket is the fastest way to make an uploaded file display, so that is what gets built.
topics.checklist: Private files are in private buckets

topics.topic: Nothing stops one person from hammering your app's most expensive feature
symptoms: AI or email feature open to everyone
topics.cause: Without rate limits, a single script can call an endpoint thousands of times. On features that cost money per call, that becomes your bill.
fixes: Limit requests per user and per IP
Require login for paid features
Set spending caps on the API provider
check: List features that cost money per use
Check whether a user can trigger them without limit
Check your provider has a spending cap
topics.prompt_fails: Limits are never part of the feature request, so they are never part of the result.
topics.checklist: Costly features have rate limits and spending caps

topics.topic: Your form checks happen only in the browser
symptoms: Bad data still ends up in the database
Empty or huge values break pages
topics.cause: Browser validation is for convenience. Anyone can skip it and send data straight to your API, so the server or database must check it again.
fixes: Validate on the server or in database constraints
Set column types, lengths and not-null rules
Reject what does not fit
check: Look at a few rows in your database
Spot empty, huge, or malformed values
Check your columns have length and required rules
prompts: Show an error if the email is wrong
topics.prompt_fails: 'Add validation' usually means messages in the form. The database still accepts whatever arrives.
topics.checklist: The server rejects bad data, not just the form

topics.topic: Customers get charged twice when they double-click pay
topics.cause: If nothing makes the payment request idempotent, two clicks or a retried request create two charges. Stripe supports idempotency keys for exactly this.
fixes: Disable the button while paying
Send an idempotency key with the request
Make the webhook handler ignore events it already processed
check: Look in Stripe for twin charges seconds apart
Check whether your pay button disables after one click
Check your webhook ignores repeats
topics.prompt_fails: Disabling the button helps, but retries and repeated webhooks happen on the server, where the screen fix cannot reach.
topics.checklist: Payments cannot be charged twice

topics.topic: Your app was fast with 10 users and crawls with 1,000 rows
topics.cause: Without indexes on the columns you filter and sort by, the database reads every row on every request. It is invisible with test data and painful with real data.
fixes: Index the columns used in filters and joins
Paginate long lists
Check slow queries in the database dashboard
check: Open your database's slow query report
Note which queries take longest
Check whether their filter columns have indexes
topics.prompt_fails: Speed problems from missing indexes live in the database. Rewriting the page around them barely moves the number.
topics.checklist: Columns you filter and sort by are indexed

topics.topic: One page of your app makes a hundred database calls
symptoms: One page is much slower than the rest
Lots of identical requests in the network tab
topics.cause: Generated code often loads a list, then fetches related data one row at a time. That is one request per item instead of one request for the whole page.
fixes: Fetch related data in one query with a join or select
Batch requests
Measure the page before and after
check: Open the slow page with dev tools, Network tab
Count the requests the page makes
Dozens of near-identical requests is the pattern
topics.prompt_fails: The AI tends to add a loading spinner or caching. The real fix is fewer requests, which means changing how the data is fetched.

topics.topic: Your app fails silently, so you only hear about bugs from angry users
symptoms: No idea how often it happens
topics.cause: If errors are caught and ignored, the user sees nothing and you get no record. You cannot fix what you cannot see.
fixes: Show a clear error to the user
Log errors to a monitoring tool
Get alerted when error rates spike
check: Search your code for empty catch blocks
Turn off your Wi-Fi and press a few buttons
If nothing tells you it failed, users get nothing either
topics.prompt_fails: 'Make the error go away' is often solved by hiding it. The failure still happens; now nobody sees it.
topics.checklist: Errors are shown to users and logged for you

topics.topic: Your backend function runs for anyone, logged in or not
topics.cause: A serverless function that does not check who is calling it will do its work for anyone who finds the URL, including sending emails or spending credits.
fixes: Require a valid user token
Check the user's permissions inside the function
Keep secrets in the function's environment
check: List your Edge Functions
For each, check it verifies the user's token
Check whether it is set to require authentication
prompts: Create a function to send the email
topics.prompt_fails: A 401 is the function refusing an unknown caller. Removing the check fixes the error and opens the door.
topics.checklist: Every backend function checks who is calling

topics.topic: One bad prompt could delete your production data and you have no backup plan
symptoms: The AI can run database changes
Prototype and production share one database
topics.cause: If development changes run against the same database real users depend on, one wrong migration can delete real data. A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a plan.
fixes: Separate development and production databases
Check what backups your plan includes
Practise a restore once
check: Check whether your builder edits your production database
Check what backups your database plan includes
Check when you last restored one
topics.prompt_fails: The AI runs the change you asked for against whatever database it is connected to. If that is production, there is no undo.
topics.checklist: Production has backups, and you have restored one

topics.topic: How to tell if your AI-built app needs fixing or rebuilding
symptoms: Every change takes longer than the last
topics.cause: Most AI-built apps are fixable: the problems cluster in a few places like auth, database rules and payments. A rebuild only makes sense when the structure itself fights every change. The way to know is to read the code, not to guess.
fixes: Get the code out of the builder into GitHub
Have someone read it and list the real problems
Decide fix or rebuild from that list
prompts: Rebuild the whole app from scratch
topics.prompt_fails: A rebuild by the same tool tends to recreate the same weak spots, just in fresh files.
